editorialDecl.p: EEBO-TCP is a partnership between the Universities of Michigan and Oxford and the publisher ProQuest to create accurately transcribed and encoded texts based on the image sets published by ProQuest via their Early English Books Online (EEBO) database (http://eebo.chadwyck.com). The general aim of EEBO-TCP is to encode one copy (usually the first edition) of every monographic English-language title published between 1473 and 1700 available in EEBO.

EEBO-TCP aimed to produce large quantities of textual data within the usual project restraints of time and funding, and therefore chose to create diplomatic transcriptions (as opposed to critical editions) with light-touch, mainly structural encoding based on the Text Encoding Initiative (http://www.tei-c.org).

The EEBO-TCP project was divided into two phases. The 25,368 texts created during Phase 1 of the project (2000-2009), initially available only to institutions that contributed to their creation, were released into the public domain on 1 January 2015. The approximately 40,000 texts produced during Phase 2 (2009- ), of which 34,963 had been released as of 2020, originally similarly restricted, were similarly freed from all restrictions on 1 August 2020. As of that date anyone is free to take and use these texts for any purpose (modify them, annotate them, distribute them, etc.). But we do respectfully request that due credit and attribution be given to their original source.
Users should be aware of the process of creating the TCP texts, and therefore of any assumptions that can be made about the data.

Text selection was based on the New Cambridge Bibliography of English Literature (NCBEL). If an author (or for an anonymous work, the title) appears in NCBEL, then their works are eligible for inclusion. Selection was intended to range over a wide variety of subject areas, to reflect the true nature of the print record of the period. In general, first editions of a works in English were prioritized, although there are a number of works in other languages, notably Latin and Welsh, included and sometimes a second or later edition of a work was chosen if there was a compelling reason to do so.

Image sets were sent to external keying companies for transcription and basic encoding. Quality assurance was then carried out by editorial teams in Oxford and Michigan. 5% (or 5 pages, whichever is the greater) of each text was proofread for accuracy and those which did not meet QA standards were returned to the keyers to be redone. After proofreading, the encoding was enhanced and/or corrected and characters marked as illegible were corrected where possible up to a limit of 100 instances per text. Any remaining illegibles were encoded as <gap>s. Understanding these processes should make clear that, while the overall quality of TCP data is very good, some errors will remain and some readable characters will be marked as illegible. Users should bear in mind that in all likelihood such instances will never have been looked at by a TCP editor.
The texts were encoded and linked to page images in accordance with level 4 of the TEI in Libraries guidelines.

Copies of the texts have been issued variously as SGML (TCP schema; ASCII text with mnemonic sdata character entities); displayable XML (TCP schema; characters represented either as UTF-8 Unicode or text strings within braces); or lossless XML (TEI P5, characters represented either as UTF-8 Unicode or TEI g elements).
Keying and markup guidelines are available at the Text Creation Partnership web site.
This file is the EEBO-TCP transcription with editorial layers added inline; nothing of the transcription has been removed.

choice/orig holds the text as printed; choice/reg holds the modern reading. reg/@resp says who decided it (#auto = machine, #editor = reviewed by hand); reg/@type is spelling, case, punctuation, spacing, grammar (an archaic form modernized: thou, hath, -eth) or emendation (another word, or a word added or removed). Where the editor overrode the machine, the editor's reg comes first and the machine's proposal follows as a second reg[@resp='#auto'].
choice/abbr + choice/expan: macron abbreviations (e.g. frō = from) and superscript contractions (yᵉ = the).
supplied: letters or words lost to illegible print, with @cert and a comment giving the evidence; the TCP gap element is kept inside.

Spelling regularized: u/v, i/j, silent final e, doubled consonants, -ie to -y, -nesse to -ness, and a word list. Grammatical forms (hath, doth, thou, thee, thy, ye, shalt, wilt, art, hast, dost) are retained. Footnote text is left in original spelling.
list[@change='#review']: run-in enumerations (I. ... II. ...) set out as numbered lists; the printed numerals are kept in label.
head[@type='edition']: section title used by this edition; the printed heading is kept in the preceding head. @change='#review' points at the revisionDesc entry for these structural changes.
Line breaks are those of the TCP transcription (newlines in the text; g[@ref='char:EOLhyphen'] marks a word hyphenated at line end). pb/@n is the printed page, pb/@facs the page image.
note/@target points at the anchor where this edition places the note; the note itself stays where it was printed.

@prev/@next link blocks this edition runs together into one paragraph; they stay separate elements as printed.

div.head: THE EPISTLE DedicatorieDedicatory. TO HIS Most Dear and Precious Ones, The Sons and Daughters of the moſtmost High God, over whom the holy GhoſtGhost hath made him a Watchman.
div.p:
CHriſtChrist, the Scripture, your owneown hearts, and SatansSatan's Devicesdevices, are the fourefour prime things that ſhouldshould be firſtfirst and moſtmost ſtudiedstudied & ſearchedsearched; if any caſtcast off the ſtudystudy of theſethese,
they cannot be ſafesafe here, nor happiehappyIf a MiniſterMinister had as many eyes as Argus, to watch; as many heads as Typheus to diſpoſedispose, and as many hands as Briareus to labour, he might findefind imploymentemployment enough for them all. hereafter. 'Tis’Tis my workework as a ChriſtianChristian, but much more as I am a watchman, to doedo my beſtbest, to diſcoverdiscover the fulneſſefulness of ChriſtChrist, the emptineſſeemptiness of the creature, and the ſnaressnares of the great Deceiverdeceiver; which I have endeavoured to doedo (in the following diſcourſediscourse) according to that meaſuremeasure of grace, which I have received from the Lord. God once accepted a handfullhandful of mealemeal for a ſacrificesacrifice; and a gripe of Goatsgoats'goats hairehair for an oblation; and I know that you have not ſoso learned the Father, as to deſpiſedespise the day of ſmallsmall things. Beloved, Satan being fallen from light to darkneſſedarkness, from felicity to miſerymisery, from Heavenheaven to hell, from an Angellangelangell to a Devilldevil, is ſoso full of malice and envy, that he will leave no meanesmeans unattempted, whereby he may make all others eternalyeternally miſerablemiserable with himſelfehimself; he being ſhutshut out of Heavenheaven, and ſhutshut up under chaineschains of darkneſſedarkness till the judgement of the great day, makes uſeuse
of all his power and skill, to bring all the ſonssons of men into the ſamesame condition, and condemnation with himſelfehimself. Satan hath caſtcast ſuchsuch ſinfullsinful ſeedseed into our ſoulessouls, that now he can no ſoonersooner tempt, but we are ready to aſſentassent; he can no ſoonersooner have a plot upon us, but he makes a conqueſtconquest of us; if he doth but ſhewshow men a little of the beauty, and bravery of the world, how ready are they to fall down, and worſhipworship him.

What ever ſinsin the heart of man is moſtmost prone to, that the Devilldevil will help forward. If Peter be ſlaviſhlyslavishlyMatth. 16. ver. 22.. ch. 26. ch. 69. ult. fearfullfearful, Satan will put him upon rebuking and denying of ChriſtChrist, to ſavesave his owneown skin. If AhabsAhab's 1 Kings 22. Prophetsprophets be given to flatter, the Devilldevil will ſtraitstrait waystraightway become a lying ſpiritspirit in the mouthesmouths of fourefour hundred of them, and they ſhallshall flatter Ahab to his ruineruin. If Judas willJohn 13. 2. be a Traitortraitor, Satan will quickly
enter into his heart, and make him ſellsell his Maſtermaster for money, which ſomesome Heathensheathens would never have done. If Ananias will lyelieActs 5. 3. for advantage, Satan wilwill fill his heart that he may lyelie (with a witneſswitness) to the Holy GhoſtGhost. Satan loves to ſailesail with the windewind, and to ſuitesuitsuite mensmen's temptations to their conditions, and inclinations; if they be in proſperityprosperity, he will tempt them to deny God; if they be in adverſityadversity, he will tempt them to diſtruſtdistrustProv. 30. v. 9. God; if their knowledge be weak, he will tempt them to have low thoughts of God; if their conſcienceconscience be tender, he will tempt to ſcrupuloſityscrupulosity; if large, to carnallcarnal ſecuritysecurity; if we be bold-ſpiritedspirited, he will tempt to preſumptionpresumption; if timeroustimorous, to deſperationdesperation; if flexible, to inconſtancieinconstancy, if ſtiffestiff, to impenitency, &etcc.

From the power, malice, and skill of Satan, doth proceed all the ſoulesoul killing plots, devices, ſtratagemsstratagems, and machinations, that be in the world; SeverallSeveral devices
he hath to draw ſoulessouls to ſinsin, and ſeverallseveral plots he hath to keepekeep ſoulessouls from all holy, and heavenly ſervicesservices; and ſeverallseveral ſtratagemsstratagems he hath, to keep ſoulessouls in a mourning, ſtaggeringstaggering, doubting, and queſtioningquestioning condition. He hath ſeverallseveral devices, to deſtroydestroy the great, and honourable, the wiſewise, and learned; the blindeblind, and ignorant; the rich, and the poorepoor; the reallreal, and the nominallnominal Saintssaints, &etcc. One while he will refrainerefrain from tempting, that we may think our ſelvesselves ſecuresecure, and neglect our watch; another while he will ſeemeseem to fliefly, that he may make us proud of the victory; one while heehe will fix mensmen's eyes more on othersothers' ſinssins, thenthan their own, that he may puffepuff them; another while he will fix their eyes more on othersothers' graces thenthan their own, that he may overwhelmeoverwhelm them &etcc. A man may as well tell the ſtarsstars, and number the ſandssands of the ſeasea, as reckon up all the devices of Satan; yet thoſethose which are moſtmost conſiderableconsiderable,
and by which he doth moſtmost miſchiefemischief to the precious ſoulessouls of men, are in the following Treatiſetreatise diſcovereddiscovered, and the Remediesremedies againſtagainst them preſcribedprescribed, &etcc.

Beloved, I think it neceſſarynecessary to give you, and the world a faithfullfaithful account of the Reaſonsreasons, moving me to appear in Printprint, in theſethese dayesdays, wherein we may ſaysay there was never more writing, and yet neverleſſenever lessneverless practiſingpractising, and they are theſethese that follow, &etcc.

FirſtFirst, becauſebecause Satan hath a1. ReaſonReason. greater influence upon men, and higher advantages over men (having the windewind and the hill as it were) thenthan they thinkethink he hath, and the knowledge of his high advantages is the high way to diſappointdisappoint him, and to render the ſoulsoul ſtrongstrong in reſiſtingresisting, and happy in conquering, &etcc.

Your importunity, and the importunity2. ReaſonReason. of many other precious ſonssons of Zion hath after much ſtrivingstriving with God, my own heart, and others, made a conqueſtconquest of
me and forced me to doedo that at laſtlast, which at firſtfirst was not a little contrary to my inclination, and reſolutionresolution, &etcc.

The ſtrangestrange oppoſitionopposition that I 3. ReaſonReason. Pirates make the ſtrongeſtstrongest and the hotteſthottest oppoſitionsoppositions againſtagainst thoſethose veſſellsvessels that are moſtmost richly laden; ſoso doth Satan that arch Pirate againſtagainst thoſethose truths, that have moſtmost of God, ChriſtChrist, and Heaven in them. met with from Satan, in the ſtudystudy of this following diſcourſediscourse, hath put an edge upon my ſpiritspirit, knowing that Satan ſtrivesstrives mightily, to keep thoſethose things from ſeeingseeing the light, that tend eminently to ſhakeshake and break his Kingdomekingdom of darkneſſedarkness, and to lift up the Kingdomekingdom and glory of the Lord JeſusJesus ChriſtChrist, in the ſoulessouls and lives of the children of men, &etcc.

Its exceeding uſefulneſſeusefulness to all ſortssorts, ranks, and conditions of men4. ReaſonReason. in the world; here you have ſalvesalve for every ſoresore, and a plaiſterplaster for every wound, and a Remedyremedy againſtagainst every diſeaſedisease; eſpeciallyespecially againſtagainst thoſethose, that tend moſtmost to the undoing of ſoulessouls, and to the ruineruin of the Statestate, &etcc.

I know not of any one, or5. ReaſonReason. other that have writ of this Subjectsubject; all that I have ever ſeenseen,
have only touchttouched upon this ſtringstring, which hath been no ſmallsmall provocation to me, to attempt to doedo ſomethingsomething this way, that others, that have better heads and hearts, may be the more ſtirredstirred to improve their Talentstalents, in a further diſcoverydiscovery of SatansSatan's Devicesdevices, and in the making knowneknown of ſuchsuch choice Remediesremedies, as may inableenable the ſoulessouls of men to triumph over all his plots and ſtratagemsstratagems, &etcc.

I have many precious friends in6 ReaſonReason. ſeverallseveral Countriescountries, who are not a little deſirousdesirous, that my pen may reach them, now my voice cannot. I have formerly been, by the help of the mightiemighty God of Jacob, a weakeweak inſtrumentinstrument of good to them, and cannot but hope, and beleevebelieve, that the Lord will alſoalso bleſſebless theſethese labours to them, they being (in part) the fruit of their deſiresdesires, and prayers, &etcc.

LaſtlyLastly, not knowing how ſoonsoon7. ReaſonReason. my Glaſſeglass may be out, and how ſoonesoon I may be cut off by a hand of death, from all opportunities of
doing further ſerviceservice for ChriſtChrist, or your ſoulessouls in this world, I was willing to ſowsow a little handfullhandful of ſpirituallspiritual ſeedseed among you; that ſoso, when I put off this earthly Tabernacletabernacle, my love to you, and that dearedear remembrance of you, which I have in my ſoulesoul, may ſtronglystrongly engage your minds and ſpiritsspirits, to make this Book your Companioncompanion; and under all externallexternal, or internallinternal changes, to make uſeuse of this heavenly Salvesalve, which I hope, will by the bleſſingblessing of the Lord, be as effectualleffectual for the healing of all your Woundswounds, as their looking up to the brazen Serpentserpent, was effectualleffectual to healeheal theirs that were bit, and ſtungstung with fiery Serpentsserpents. I ſhallshall leave this Book with you, as a Legacielegacy of my deareſtdearest Lovelove, deſiringdesiring the Lord to make it a far greater, and ſweetersweeter Legacielegacy, thenthan all thoſethose carnallcarnal Legacieslegacies are, that are left by the high and mighty ones of the earth, to their neareſtnearest and deareſtdearest relations, &etcc.

Beloved, I would not have affection carriecarry my pen too much beyond my intention; therefore onelyonly give me leave to ſignifiesignify my deſiresdesires for you, and my deſiresdesires to you; and I ſhallshall draw to a cloſeclose.

My deſiresdesires for you are, That he would grant you according to the riches EpheſEphes. 3. of his glory, to be ſtrengthnedstrengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner VerſVers. 17. man. That ChriſtChrist may dwell in your hearts by faith, that ye being rooted and grounded in love; May be able to VerſVers. 18. comprehend with all Saintssaints, what is the breadth, and length, and depth, VerſVers. 19. and height: And to know the love of ChriſtChrist that paſſethpasseth knowledge; That ye might be filled with all the fullneſſefulnessfullness of God. And that yeeye might walkewalk ColoſColos. 1. 10. worthy of the Lord unto all pleaſingpleasing, being fruitfullfruitful in every good workework, and increaſedincreased in the knowledge of God, StrengthnedStrengthened with all might, according VerſVers. 11. to his glorious power, unto all patience, and long-ſufferingsuffering with joyfullneſſejoyfulnessjoyfullness. That ye doedo no evillevil. That 2 Cor. 13. 7. your love may abound yet more and more in Knowledge, and in all Judgementjudgement. Phil. 1. 9.
That yeeye may approve things that are excellent, that ye may be ſinceresincere, VerſVers. 10. and without offence till the day of ChriſtChrist. And that our God would 2 TheſſThess. 1. 11. count you worthy of this calling, and fulfill all the good pleaſurepleasure of his goodneſſegoodness, and the workework of Faithfaith with VerſVers. 12. power. That the name of our Lord JeſusJesus ChriſtChrist may be glorified in you, and ye in him, according to the grace of our God, and the Lord JeſusJesus ChriſtChrist. And that you may be eminent inPſalPsal. 93. 5. Sanctitiesanctity; Sanctitiesanctity being ZionsZion's glory, that your hearts may be kept upright, your judgements ſoundsound, and your lives unblamable. That as you are now my joy, ſoso in the day of ChriſtChrist you may be my Crowncrown; That I may ſeesee my labours in your lives, that your converſationconversation may not be earthly, when the things you hearehear are heavenly; but that it may be as becomes the Goſpelgospel. That as the Fiſhesfishes which live in the ſaltsalt Sea, yet are freſhfresh; ſoso you, though you live in an uncharitable world, may yet be charitable and loving. That ye may
like the BeebeeBe, ſucksuck Honeyhoney out of every Flowerflower; That ye may ſhineshine in a ſeasea of troubles, as the Pearlepearl ſhinesshines in the ſkiesky, though it grows in the Sea; That in all your trials you may be like the ſtonestone in Thracia, that neither burneth in the fire, nor ſinkethsinketh in the water. That ye may be like the Heavensheavens, excellent in ſubſtancesubstance, and beautifullbeautiful in appearance; that ſoso you may meet me with joy, in that day, wherein ChriſtChrist ſhallshall ſaysay to his Father, LoeLo, here am I, and the children that thou haſthast given me.

My deſiresdesires to you are, That you would make it your buſineſſebusiness to ſtudystudy ChriſtChrist, his Word, your own Heartshearts, SatansSatan's Plotsplots, and Eternityeternity, more thenthan ever; that ye would endeavour more to be inwardly ſinceresincere, thenthan outwardly glorious; to live, thenthan to have a name to live. That yeeye would labour with all your might, to be thankfullthankful under Merciesmercies, and faithfullfaithful in your Placesplaces, and humble under Divinedivine Appearancesappearances, and fruitfullfruitful under
precious Ordinancesordinances; that as your meanesmeans and mercies are greater thenthan others, ſoso your account before God may not prove worſeworse thenthan others. That ye would pray for me, who am not worthy to be named among the Saintssaints, that I may be a precious inſtrumentinstrument in the hand of ChriſtChrist, to bring in many ſoulessouls unto him, and to build up thoſethose that are brought in, in their moſtmost holy Faithfaith; And that Utteranceutterance may be given to me, that I may make knowneknown all the will of God. That2 Cor. 11. 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28. I may be ſinceresincere, faithfullfaithful, frequent, fervent, and conſtantconstant in the workework of the Lord, and that my labour be not in vainevain in the Lord; That my Labourslabours may be accepted of the Lord, and his Saintssaints, and I may daily ſeesee the travelltravailtravel of my ſoulesoul, &etcc.

But above all, pray for me, that I may more and more findefind the power, and ſweetsweet of thoſethose things upon my owneown heart, that I give out to you and others; and that my ſoulesoul be ſoso viſitedvisited with ſtrengthstrength
from on high, that I may live up fully, and conſtantlyconstantly to thoſethose truths that I hold forth to the world; and that I may be both in Lifelife and Doctrinedoctrine, a burning and a ſhiningshining light; That ſoso, when the Lord JeſusJesus ſhallshall appear, I may receive a crown of glory, which he ſhallshall give to me in that day, and not onelyonly to me, but to all that love his appearing, &etcc.

For a cloſeclose, remember this, that your life is ſhortshort, your duties many, your aſſiſtanceassistance great, and your reward ſuresure; therefore faint not, hold on, and hold up in wayesways of well doing, and Heavenheaven ſhallshall make amends for all.
I ſhallshall now take leave of you, when my heart hath by my hand ſubſcribedsubscribed that I am,

div.head: A WORD TO THE READER.

div.head: Now the Remedies againſtagainst this Device of Satan are theſethese.

FIrſtFirst, ConſiderConsider that ſinsin is never a whit1 Remedy. the leſſeless filthy, vildevile, and abominable, by its being coloured and painted with vertuesvirtue'svirtues colours. div.head: Now the Remedies againſtagainst this device of Satan are theſethese.
div.p:
FIrſtFirst, ſolemnlysolemnly conſiderconsider, that thoſethose1. Remedy. ſinssins, which we are apt to account ſmallsmall, hath brought upon men the greateſtgreatest wrath of God; as the eating of an Appleapple; gathering a few ſtickssticks on
the SabbaothSabbath day, and touching of the Arkark; oh! the dreadfulldreadful wrath that theſethese ſinnessins brought down, upon the Draco the Rigid Law-giver, being asked why, when ſinssins were not equallequal, he appointed death to all? AnſweredAnswered, he knew that ſinssins were not all equallequal; but he knew the leaſtleast deſerveddeserved death. So though the ſinssins of men hebe not all equallequal, yet the leaſtleast of them deſervesdeserves eternalleternal death. heads, and hearts of men; the leaſtleast ſinsin is contrary to the Lawlaw of God, the nature of God, the being of God, and the glory of God, and therefore tis’tis often puniſhedpunished ſeverelyseverely by God; and doedo not we ſeesee daily the vengeance of the Almighty falling upon the bodies, names, eſtatesestates, Familiesfamilies, and ſoulessouls of men for thoſethose ſinssins, that are but little ones in their eyes. Surely, if we are not utterly left of God, and blinded by Satan, we cannot but ſeesee it. Oh! therefore, when Satan ſaiessays tis’tis but a little one, doedo thou ſaysay, oh! but thoſethose ſinssins that thou calleſtcallest little, are ſuchsuch, that will cauſecause God to rainerain Hellhell out of Heavenheaven upon ſinnerssinners, as he did upon the Sodomites.

ſinsin, as we pleaſpleasepleas, and we by yeildingyielding to thePſalPsal. 137. ver. 9. Happy ſhallshall he be that taketh and daſhethdasheth thy little ones againſtagainst the ſtonesstones. The ſeventhseventh Remedyremedy againſtagainst this Devicedevice,7 Remedy. is ſolemnlysolemnly to conſiderconsider, That there is more evillevil in the leaſtleast ſinsin, thenthan in the greateſtgreatest affliction; and this appears as clear as the Sunsun, by the ſeveresevere dealing of God the Father, with his beloved Son, who let all the vials of his fierceſtfiercest wrath upon him, and that for the leaſtleast ſinsin as well as for the greateſtgreatest; The wages Death is the hire of the leaſtleast ſinsin; the beſtbest wages that the leaſtleast ſinsin gives his ſouldierssoldiers, is death of all ſortssorts; in a ſtrictstrict ſencesensesence, there is no ſinsin little, becauſebecause no little God to ſinsin againſtagainst. of ſinsin is death, of ſinsin indefinitely, whether great or ſmallsmall; Oh! how ſhouldshould this make us tremble, as much at the leaſtleast ſparkspark of luſtlust, as at hell it ſelfeself? ConſideringConsidering that God the Father would not ſparespare his boſomebosom Son, no, not for the leaſtleast ſinsin; but would make him drink the dregs of his wrath. And ſoso much for the Remediesremedies that may fence and preſervepreserve our ſoulssouls from being drawn to ſinsin, by this third Devicedevice of Satan.

The fourth Devicedevice that Satan hath4 Device. to draw the ſoulsoul to ſinsin, is, by preſentingpresenting to the ſoulsoul the beſtbest mensmen's ſinssins, and by hiding from the ſoulsoul their virtues; by ſhewingshowing the ſoulsoul their ſinssins, and by hiding from the ſoulsoul, their ſorrows • sorrows, and r • epe • ntance; as by ſettingsetting before the ſoulsoul the Adulteryadultery of David, the Pridepride of

div.head: Now the Remedies againſtagainst this Device of the Devil are theſethese that follow.

The ſecondsecond Remedyremedy againſtagainst this Devicedevice2 Remedy. of Satan, is, ſolemnlysolemnly to conſiderconsider, that theſethese Saintssaints did not make a trade of ſinsin, they fell once, or twice (and roſerose by Repentancerepentance) that they mightThe Saints cannot ſinsin (voluntate plenâ ſedsed ſemiplenasemiplena) with a whole will, but as it were with an halfehalf will, an unwilling willingneswillingness, not with a full conſentconsent, but with a diſſentingdissenting conſentconsent. keep the cloſercloser to ChriſtChrist for ever; they fell accidentally, occaſionallyoccasionally, and with much reluctancy; and thou ſinneſtsinnest preſumptuouſlypresumptuously, obſtinatelyobstinately, readily, delightfully, and cuſtomarilycustomarily; thou haſthast by thy making a trade of ſinsin, contracted upon thy ſoulsoul a kind of curſedcursed neceſſitynecessity of ſinningsinning, that thou canſtcanst as well ceaſecease to be, or ceaſecease to live, as thou canſtcanst ceaſecease to ſinsin; ſinsin is by cuſtomecustom become as another nature to thee, which thou canſtcanst not, which thou wilt not lay aſideaside,
though thou knoweſtknowest, that if thou doſtdost not lay ſinsin aſideaside, God will lay thy ſoulsoul aſideaside for ever; though thou knoweſtknowest, that if ſinsin and thy ſoulsoul doedo not part, ChriſtChrist and thy ſoulsoul can never meet; if thou wilt make a trade of ſinsin, and cry out, did not David ſinsin thus, and Noah
2 Pet. 2. 14. Pro. 44. 14, 14. 16. Though ſinsin doedo (habitare) dwell in the regenerate, as AuſtinAugustineAustin notes, yet it doth not (regnare) reign over the regenerate, they riſerise by repentance. ſinsin thus, and Peter ſinsin thus, &etcc.? No, their hearts turn'd aſideaside to folly one day, but thy heart turns aſideaside to folly every day, and when they were fallen, they riſerise by repentance, and by the actings of Faithfaith upon a crucified ChriſtChrist, but thou falleſtfallest, and haſthast no ſtrengthstrength, nor will to riſerise; but walloweſtwallowest in ſinsin, and wilt eternally dyedie in thy ſinssins, unleſſeunless the Lord be the more mercifullmerciful to thy ſoulsoul. DoſtDost thou think, oh ſoulesoul, this is good reaſoningreasoning? Such a one taſtedtasted poyſonpoison but once, and yet narrowly eſcaptescapt, but I doedo daily drink poyſonpoison, yet I ſhallshall eſcapeescape: yet ſuchsuch is the mad reaſoningreasoning of vainevain ſoulessouls; David and Peter, &etcc. ſinnedsinnedSinned once foully and fearfully, they taſtedtasted poyſonpoison but once, and were ſicksick to death, but I taſttaste it daily, and yet ſhallshall not taſttaste of eternalleternal death. The fourth Remedyremedy againſtagainst this Devicedevice4 Remedy. of Satan, is, ſolemnlysolemnly to conſiderconsider, That there are but two main ends of GodsGod's recording of the falsfalls of his Saintssaints; and the one is, to keep thoſethose from fainting,I have known a good man, ſaidsaid Bernard, who when he heard of any, that had committed ſomesome notorious ſinsin, he was wont to ſ • aysay with himſelfehimself (ille bodiehodiebody & ego cras) he fell to day, ſoso may I to morrow. ſinkingsinking, and deſpairedespair, under the burden of their ſinssins, who fall through weakneſſeweakness and infirmity; and the other is, that their falls may be as Landmarkslandmarks, to warn others that ſtandstand, to take heed leſtlest they fall; it never entredentered into the heart of God to record his ChildrensChildren's ſinssins, that others might be incouragedencouraged to ſinsin, but that others might be warned to look to their ſtandingsstandings, and to hang the faſterfaster upon the skirts of ChriſtChrist, and avoid all occaſionsoccasions and temptations, that may occaſionoccasion the ſoulsoul to fall, as others have fallen. When they have been left by ChriſtChrist, the Lord hath made their ſinssins as Landland-marks, to warn his people to take heed how they come near thoſethose ſandssands, and rocks; thoſethose ſnaressnares and baitesbaits that have been fatal to the choyceſtchoicest treaſurestreasures, to wit, the joy, peace, comfort, and glorious enjoyments of the braveſtbravest ſpiritsspirits, and nobleſtnoblest
ſoulssouls that ever ſailedsailed through the ocean of this ſinfullsinful, troubleſometroublesome world; as you may ſeesee in David, Job, Peter, &etcc. There is nothing in the world, that can ſoso notoriouſlynotoriously croſſecross the grand end of GodsGod's recording of the ſinssins of his Saintssaints, thenthan for any from thence, to take incouragementencouragement to ſinsin, and where ever you find ſuchsuch a ſoulsoul, you may write him ChriſtleſſeChristless, Graceleſſegraceless, a ſoulsoul caſtcast off by God, a ſoulesoul that Satan hath by the hand; and the eternalleternal God knowesknows whetherwhither he will lead him.

The fifth Devicedevice that Satan hath, to5 Device. draw the ſoulsoul to ſinsin, is, to preſentpresent God to the ſoulsoul, as one made up all of mercy; oh! ſaithsaith Satan, you need not make ſuchsuch a matter of ſinsin, you need not be ſoso fearfullfearful of ſinsin, nor ſoso unwilling to ſinsin; for God is a God of mercy, a God full of mercy, a God that delights in mercy, a God that is ready to ſhewshow mercy, a God that is never weary of ſhewingshowing mereymercy, a God more prone to pardon his people, thenthan to puniſhpunish his people; and therefore he will not take advantage againſtagainst the ſoulesoul, and why then, ſaithsaith Satan, ſhouldshould you make ſuchsuch a matter of ſinsin?

div.head: Now the Remedies againſtagainst this Device of Satan are theſethese.
div.p:
THeThe firſtfirst Remedyremedy is, ſeriouſlyseriously to conſiderconsider,1 Remedy. that 'tis’tis the ſoreſtsorest judgement in this world, to be left to ſinsin upon any pretence whatſoeverwhatsoever; oh! unhappy man, when God leaveth thee to thy Humanum eſtest peccare, Diaboli cumDiabolicum perſeverareperseverare, & AngelicūAngelicumAngelicumAngelicun reſurgereresurgere (AuſtinAugustineAustin) i. e. It is a humanehuman thing to fall into ſinsin, a divel • iſhdevilish to perſeverepersevere therein, and an AngellcalAngelical or ſupernaturalsupernatural to riſerise from it. ſelfself, and doth not reſiſtresist thee in thy ſinssins; woe, woe to him, at whoſewhose ſinssins God doth wink: when God lets the way to Hellhell be a ſmoothsmooth and pleaſantpleasant way, that is hell on this ſideside hell, and a dreadfulldreadful ſignesign of GodsGod's indignation againſtagainst a man; a token of his rejection, and that God doth not intend good unto him; that is a ſadsad word, Ephraim is joynedjoined to Idolsidols, let him alone, he will be uncounſellableuncounsellable, and uncorrigible, he hath made a match with miſchiefemischief, he ſhallshall have his belly-full of it, he falls with open eyes, let him fall at his owneown perrillperil; and that's a terrible ſayingsaying, So I gave them up unto their own hearts PſalPsal. 81. 12. HoſeaHosea 4. 14. luſtslusts, and they walked in their owneown counſelscounsels. A ſoulsoul given up to ſinsin▪ is a ſoulsoul r • ipe for hell, a ſoulsoul poſtingposting to deſtructiondestruction. Ah A me, me ſlavasalvaslava Domine. Deliver me O Lord from that evil man, my ſelfself. Aug. Lord! thisThis mercy I humbly beg, that what ever thou giveſtgivest me up to, thou wilt not give me up to the wayesways of mine own heart; if thou wilt give me up to be afflicted, or tempted, or reproached,
&etcc. I will patiently ſitsit down, and ſaysay, 'Tis’tis the Lord, let him doedo with me what ſeemsseems good in his owneown eyes; doedo any thing with me, lay what burden thou wilt upon me, ſoso thou doeſtdoest not give me up to the wayesways of my own heart, &etcc.

The ſecondsecond Remedyremedy againſtagainst this Devicedevice2 Remedy. of Satan, is, ſolemnlysolemnly to conſiderconsider, that God is as juſtjust, as he is mercifullmerciful: as the Scriptures ſpeakspeak him out to be a very mercifullmerciful God, ſoso they ſpeakspeak him 2 PetPet. 2. 4, 5, 6. God hang'd them up in Gibbets, as it were, that others might hear, and fear, and doedo no more ſoso wickedly. out to be a very juſtjust God; witneſſewitness his caſtingcasting the Angelsangels out of Heavenheaven, and his binding them in chains of darkneſſedarkness, till the judgement of the great day; and witneſſewitness his turning Adam out of ParadiſeParadise; his drowning of the old world; and his raining Hellhell out of Heavenheaven upon SodomeSodom; and witneſſewitness all the croſſescrosses, loſſeslosses, ſickneſſessicknesses, and diſeaſesdiseases that be in the world; and witneſſewitness Tophet that is prepared of old, witneſſewitness his treaſuringtreasuring up of wrath, againſtagainst the day of wrath, unto the revelation of the juſtjust judgements of God; but above all, witneſſewitness the pouring forth of all his wrath upon his boſomebosom Son, when he did bare the ſinssins of his people, and cryedcried out, My God, my God, why haſthast thou forſakenforsaken -me? Mat. 27. 46.

The third Remedyremedy againſtagainst this Devicedevice3 Remedy. of Satan, is, ſeriouſlyseriously to conſiderconsider, that
ſinssins againſtagainst mercy, will bring the greateſtgreatest, and the ſoreſtsorest judgements upon mensmen's heads and hearts; Mercymercy is Alpha, Juſticejustice is Omega; David ſpeakingspeaking of theſethese Attributesattributes, placeth Mercymercy in the foreward, and Juſticejustice in the rereward, ſayingsaying, My Song ſhallshall be of Mercymercy and Judgementjudgement; PſalPsal. 101. 1. when Mercymercy is deſpiſeddespised, then Juſticejustice takes the Thronethrone. God is like a Quantò gradus altior tantò caſuscasus gravior, the higher we are indignityin dignity, the more grievous is our fall and miſerymisery. Princeprince, that ſendethsendeth not his Armyarmy againſtagainst Rebelsrebels, before he hath ſentsent his Pardonpardon, and proclaimed it by a HerauldHerald of Armsarms. He firſtfirst hangs out the white Flagflag of Mercymercy, if this wins men in, they are happy for ever; but if they ſtandstand out, then God will put forth his red Flagflag of Juſticejustice and Judgementjudgement; if the one be deſpiſeddespised, the other ſhallshall be felt with a witneſſewitness; ſeesee this in the IſraelitesIsraelites,
Deus tardus eſtest ad iram ſedsed tarditatem gravitate pœ •• nae compenſatcompensat. God is ſlowslow to anger, but he recompencethrecompenseth his ſlowneſſeslowness with grievouſneſſegrievousness of puniſhmentpunishment. he loved them, and choſechose them, when they were in their blood, and moſtmost unlovely, he multiplied them, not by means, but by miracle; for from ſeventyseventy ſoulssouls, they grew in few years, to ſixsix hundred thouſandthousand; the more they were oppreſſedoppressed, the more they proſperedprospered: like Camomile, the more you tread it, the more you ſpreadspread it; or to a PalmePalm tree, the more it is preſſedpressed, the further it ſpreadethspreadeth; or to fire, the more it is raked the more it burneth; their mercies came in upon them, like Job's Meſſengersmessengers,
one upon the neck of another.If we abuſeabuse mercy to ſerveserve our luſtslusts, then in SalviansSalvian's phraſephrase, God will rain hell out of Heaven, rather thenthan not viſitvisit for ſuchsuch ſinssins. He put off their ſackcloathsackcloth, and girded them with gladneſſegladness, and compaſſedcompassed them about with ſongssongs of deliverance; he carried them on the wings of Eagles, he kept them as the Appleapple of his eye, &etcc. But they abuſingabusing his mercy, became the greateſtgreatest objects of his wrath; as, I know not the man that can reckon up their mercies: ſoso I know not the man that can ſumsum up the miſeriesmiseries that are come upon them for their ſinssins; for as our Saviour propheſiedprophesied concerning JeruſalemJerusalem, That a ſtonestone
VeſpaſianVespasian brake into their City at Cedron, where they took ChriſtChrist, on the ſamesame FeaſtFeast day that ChriſtChrist was taken. heHe whipped them where they whipped ChriſtChrist, he ſoldsold twenty Jews for a penny, as they ſouldsoldsould ChriſtChrist for 30 pence 8. Andr. cat.
ſhouldshould not be left upon a ſtonestone: ſoso it was fulfilled forty years after his Aſcenſionascension, by VeſpaſianVespasian the Emperouremperor, and his Son, Titus, who having beſie • gedbesieged JeruſalemJerusalem, the JewesJews were oppreſſedoppressed with a grievous famine, in which their food was old ſhooesshoesshoos, old leather, old hay, and the dung of Beaſtsbeasts; thenethen died partly of the Swordsword, and partly of the Faminefamine, eleven hundred thouſandthousand of the poorer ſortsort; two thouſandthousand in one night were imbowelledembowelled, ſixsix thouſandthousand were burned in a porch of the Templetemple, the whole, Citycity was ſackedsacked and burnt, and laid levelllevel to the ground, and ninety ſevenseven thouſandthousand taken Captivescaptives, and applied to baſebase and miſerablemiserable ſerviceservice; as Eu • ſebiusEusebius and JoſephusJosephus ſaithsaith: and to this • day, in all the parts of the world, are they
not the off-ſcouringscouring of the world? noneNone leſſeless belov'd, and none • more abhor'd, thenthan they: And ſoso CaparnaumCapernaum, that was lifted up to Heavenheaven, was threatnedthreatened to beMen are therforetherefore the worſworsewors, becauſebecause they ought to be better, and ſhallshall be deeper in Hell, becauſebecause Heaven was offered unto them, but they would not. Ingentia beneficia flagitia, ſuppliciasupplicia, good turnesturns aggravate unkindneſſesunkindness, and mensmen's offences are increaſedincreased by their obligation. ἀμελήσαντες 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . ſhiftshift off, diſregarddisregard. thrown down to Hellhell. No ſoulssouls fall ſoso low into Hellhell (if they fall) as thoſethose ſoulssouls, that by a hand of mercy, are lifted up neareſtnearest to Heavenheaven; you flightslight ſoulssouls that are ſoso apt to abuſeabuse mercy, conſiderconsider this, that in the Goſpelgospel dayesdays, the plagues that God inflicts upon the deſpiſersdespisers, and abuſersabusers of mercy, are uſuallyusually ſpirituallspiritual plagues; as blindneſſeblindness of mind, hardneſſehardness of heart, benumedneſſebenumbednessbenumedness of conſcienceconscience, which are ten thouſandthousand times worſeworse thenthan the worſtworst of outward plagues that can be • fall you, and therefore though you may eſcapeescape temporalltemporal Judgementsjudgements, yet you ſhallshall not eſcapeescape ſpirituallspiritual Judgementsjudgements: How ſhallshall we eſcapeescape if we neglect ſoso great ſalvationsalvation? ſaithSaith the Apoſtleapostle. Oh! therefore, when ever Satan ſhallshall preſentpresent God to the ſoulsoul, as one made up all of mercy, that he may draw thee to doedo wickedly, ſaysay unto him, that ſinssins againſtagainst mercy will bring upon the ſoulsoul the greateſtgreatest miſerymisery, and therefore, whatever becomes of thee, thou wilt not ſinsin againſtagainst mercy, &etcc.

The fourth Remedyremedy againſtagainst this Devicedevice4 Remedy. of Satan, is ſeriouſlyseriously to conſiderconsider, that though GodsGod's generallgeneral mercy be over
all his works, yet his ſpeciallspecial mercy AuguſtusAugustus in his ſolemnsolemn FeaſtsFeasts gave trifles to ſomesome, but gold to others that his heart was moſtmost ſetset upon: ſoso God by a hand of generallgeneral mercy, gives theſethese (poorepoor trifles) outward bleſſingsblessings t • o thoſethose that he leaſtleast loves, but his gold, his ſpeciallspecial mercy is onelyonly towards thoſethose that his heart is moſtmost ſetset upon. is confined to thoſethose that are divinely qualified; ſoso in Exod. 34. 6, 7. And the Lord paſſedpassed by before him, and proclaimed, the Lord, the Lord God, mercifullmerciful and gracious, long-ſufferingsuffering, and abundant in goodneſſegoodness and truth; keeping mercy for thouſandsthousands, forgiving iniquity, tranſgreſſiontransgression, and ſinsin, and that will by no means clear the guilty, Exod. 20. 6. And ſhewingshowing mercy unto thouſandsthousands of them that love me, and keep my Commandementscommandments, PſalPsal. 25. 10. All the paths of the Lord are mercy and truth: unto ſuchsuch as keep his Covenantcovenant, and his TeſtimoniesTestimonies, PſalPsal. 32. 10. Many ſorrowssorrows ſhallshall be to the wicked, but he that truſtethtrusteth in the Lord, mercy ſhallshall compaſſecompass him about, PſalPsal. 33. 18. Behold, the eye of the Lord is upon them that fear him, upon them that hope in his mercy. PſalPsal. 103. 11. For as the Heavenheaven is high above the earth: ſoso great is his mercy to as ardtoward them that fearefear him. Ver. 17. But the mercy of the Lord is from everlaſtingeverlasting, to everlaſtingeverlasting, upon them that fearefear him. When Satan attempts to draw thee to ſinsin, by preſentingpresenting God as a God all made up of mercy; oh! then reply, that thothough GodsGod's general mercy extends to all the works of his hand; yet his ſpeciallspecial mercy is confined to them that are divinely qualified, to them that love hi • m, and keep his Commandementscommandments, to
them that truſttrust in him, that by hope hang upon him, and that fear him, and that thou muſtmust be ſuchsuch a one here, or elſeelse thou canſtcanst never be happy hereafter; thou muſtmust partake of his ſpeciallspecial mercy, or elſeelse eternally periſhperish in everlaſtingeverlasting miſerymisery, notwithſtandingnotwithstanding GodsGod's generallgeneral mercy.

The fifth Remedyremedy againſtagainst this Devicedevice5 Remedy. of Satan, is, ſolemnlysolemnly to conſiderconsider, that thoſethose that were once glorious on earth, and are now triumphing in Heavenheaven, did look upon the mercy of God, as the moſtmost powerfullpowerful argument to preſervepreserve them from ſinsin, and to fence their ſoulssouls againſtagainst ſinsin, and not as an encouragementPſalPsal.Psal 26. 3, 4, 5, 6. to ſinsin. PſalPsal. 26. 3, 4, 5, 6. For thy loving kindneſſekindness is before mine eyes, and I have walked in thy truth; I have not ſatsat with vainevain perſonspersons, neither will I goego in with diſſemblersdissemblers: I have hated the Congregationcongregation of evillevil doers, and will not ſitsit with the wicked. So JoſephJoseph ſtrengthensstrengthens himſelfehimself againſtagainst ſinsin, from the remembrance of mercy. How then can I (ſaithsaith he) doedo this great Gen. 39. 9. wickedneſſewickedness, and ſinsin againſtagainst God? He had fixtfixed his eye upon mercy, and therefore ſinsin could not enter, though the irons entredentered into his ſoulsoul, his ſoulsoul being taken with mercy, was not moved by his MiſtriſſesMistress'sMistresses impudency; Satan knock't oft at the door, but the ſightsight of mercy
would not ſuffersuffer him to anſweranswer, or open: JoſephJoseph like a Pearlepearl in a Puddle, keeps his vertuevirtue ſtillstill. So Paul, Shall we continue in ſinsin that Gracegrace may abound? God
Rom. 6. 1, 2. The ſtonestone called Pa • ntaurus, is of that vertuevirtue, that it preſervespreserves him that carries it, from taking any harm by poiſonpoison; the mercy of God in ChriſtChrist to our ſoulssouls, is the moſtmost precious ſtonestone, or Pearle • Pearl in the world, to preſervepreserve us from being poyſonedpoisoned with ſinsin. forbid; how ſhallshall we that are dead to ſinsin live any longer therein? There is nothing in the world, that renders a man more unlike to a Saintsaint, and more like to Satan, thenthan to argue from mercy to ſinfullsinful liberty; from Divinedivine goodneſſegoodness to licentiouſneſſelicentiousness; this is the Devilsdevil'sdevils Logicklogic, and in whom ever you find it, you may write, This ſoulsoul is loſtlost. A man may as • truly ſaysay, the Sea burns, or fire cools, as that free grace and mercy ſhouldshould make a ſoulsoul truly gracious to doedo wickedly. So the ſamesame Apoſtleapostle, I beſeechbeseech you therefore brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye preſentpresent your bodies a living ſacrificesacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reaſonablereasonable ſerviceservice. So John, TheſeThese things I write unto you, that you ſinsin not; What was it that he wrote? He wrote, that we might have fellowſhipfellowship with the Father and his Son; 1 John 2. 1, 2. and that the Blood of ChriſtChrist cleanſethcleanseth us from all ſinsin: and that, if we confeſſeconfess our ſinssins, he is juſtjust and faith fullfaithful to forgive us our ſinssins; and that, if we doedo ſinsin, we have an Advocate with the Father, JeſusJesus ChriſtChrist the righteous. TheſeThese choycechoice favours, and mercies the Apoſtleapostle holds forth, as the choyceſtchoicest means to preſervepreserve the ſoulsoul from
ſinsin, and to keep at the greateſtgreatest diſtancedistance from ſinsin, and if this won't doedo it, you may write the man void of ChriſtChrist, and grace, and undone for ever.

The ſixtsixth Devicedevice that Satan hath to6 Device. draw the ſoulesoul to ſinsin, is, by perſwadingpersuading the ſoulsoul that the work of Repentancerepentance is a • n eaſieeasy work, and that therefore the ſoulsoul need not make ſuchsuch a matter of ſinsin; why ſuppoſesuppose you do ſinsin, ſaithsaith Satan, 'tis’tis no ſuchsuch difficult thing to return, and confeſſeconfess, and be ſorrowfullsorrowful, and beg pardon, and cry, Lord have mercy upon me; and if you doedo but this, God will cut the ſcorescore, and pardon your ſinssins, and ſavesave your ſoulssouls, &etcc. By this Devicedevice Satan draws many a ſoulsoul to ſinsin, and makes many millions of ſoulssouls ſervantsservants, or rather ſlavesslaves to ſinsin, &etcc.

div.head: Now the Remedies againſtagainst this device of Satan are theſethese that follow.
div.p:
THeThe firſtfirst Remedyremedy is, ſeriouſlyseriously to conſiderconsider, 1 Remedy. Fallen man hath loſtlost (imperium ſuumsuum, and imperium ſuisui) the command of himſelfehimself, and the command of the creatures; and certainly, he that cannot command himſelfehimself, cannot repent of himſelfehimself. Da poenitentiāpoenitentiampoenitentiampoenitentian & poſteapostea indulgentiam, ſaidsaid dying Fulgentius. that Repentancerepentance is a mighty work, a difficult work, a work that is above our power. There is no power below that power that raiſedraised ChriſtChrist from the dead, and that made the world, that can break the heart of a ſinnersinner, or turn the heart of a ſinnersinner; thou art as wellwell able to
melt Adamantadamant, as to melt thine owneown heart, to turn a flint into fleſhflesh, as to turn thine own heart to the Lord; to raiſeraise the dead, and to make a world, as to Repentrepent. Repentance is a flower that growesgrows not in Naturesnature'snatures garden. Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the Leopard his ſpotsspots, then may yeeye alſoalso doedo good, that are accuſtomedaccustomed to doedo evillevil, Jer. 13. 23. Repentance is a gift that comes down from above, men are not born with Repentancerepentance in their hearts, as they are borneborn with tongues in their mouths, Acts. 5.It was a vain brag of King Cyrus, that cauſedcaused it to be written upon his Tomb-ſtonestone (πάντα ποιεῖν ἐδυνάμην 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 ) I could doedo all things. So could Paul too, but it was through ChriſtChrist which ſtrengthnedstrengthened him. 31. Him hath God exalted with his right hand, to be a Princeprince and a Saviour, for to give Repentancerepentance to IſraelIsrael, and forgiveneſſeforgiveness of ſinssins. So in that 2 Tim. 2. 25. In meekneſſemeekness inſtructinginstructing them that oppoſeoppose themſelvesthemselves, if God peradventure will give them repentance, to the acknowledging of the truth. 'Tis’Tis not in the power of any mortallmortal to repent at pleaſurepleasure: Some ignorant, deluded ſoulssouls vainly conceit that theſethese five words, Lord have mercy upon me, are efficacious to ſendsend them to Heavenheaven; but as many are undone by buying a counterfeit Jewelljeweljewell: ſoso many are in Hellhell, by miſtakemistake of their Repentancerepentance; many reſtrest in their Repentancerepentance, though it be but the ſhadowshadow of Repentancerepentance, which cauſedcaused one to ſaysay, Repentancerepentance damneth more thenthan ſinsin.

The ſecondsecond Remedyremedy againſtagainst this Devicedevice2 Re • medy. of Satan, is, ſolemnlysolemnly to conſiderconsider of the nature of true Repentancerepentance; Repentancerepentance is ſomesome other thing thenthan what vain men conceive. Repentance is ſometimessometimes taken in a more ſtrictstrict and narrowThe Hebrew word for Repentance, is תשובה 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 from שוב 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 wchwchwhich ſignifiessignifies to returnereturn, implying a going back from what a man had dondone, it notes a returning or converting from one thing to another, from ſinsin to God. The Greeks have two words, by which they expreſſeexpress the nature of repentance, one is μεταμελεῖν 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , which ſignifiessignifies to be carefullcareful, anxious, ſolicitoussolicitous after a thing is done; the other word is μετάνοια 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , is reſipiſcentiaresipiscentia, after-wit, or after-wiſdomwisdom, the minds recovering of wiſdomewisdom, or growing wiſerwiser after our folly. Ab ἄνοια 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 dementia & μετά 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 μετάμετα poſtpost, it being the correction of mensmen's folly, and returning ad ſanamsanam mentem. True repentance is a thorough change, both of the mind and manners, optima & aptiſſimaaptissima poenitentia eſtest nova vita, ſaithsaith Luther, which ſayingsaying is an excellent ſayingsaying. Repentance for ſinsin is nothing worth, without repentance from ſinsin. If thou repent with a contradiction (ſaithsaith Tertullian) God will pardon thee with a contradiction; thou repenteſtrepentest, and yet continueſtcontinuest in thy ſinsin, God will pardon thee, and yet ſendsend thee to Hell; there's a pardon with a contradiction. Negative goodneſſegoodness ſervesserves no mansman's turn to ſavesave him from the axe. It is ſaidsaid of Ithacus, that the hatred of the PriſcillianPriscillian HereſieHeresy, was all the vertuevirtue that he had. The evillevil ſervantservant did not riot out his Talent. ThoſeThose Reprobates, Mat. 25. robbed not the Saints, but relieved them not; for this they muſtmust eternally perish ſenſesense, for godly ſorrowsorrow; ſometimessometimes Repentancerepentance is taken in a large ſenſesense, for Amendmentamendment of Lifelife. Repentance hath in it three things, viz. theThe Act, the Subjectsubject, and the TermesTerms.

1. The formallformal Act of Repentancerepentance is a changing, and converting; 'tis’tis often ſetset forth in Scripture by Turning, TurneTurn thou me, and I ſhallshall be turned, ſaithsaith Ephraim; after that I was turned, I repented, ſaithsaith he; 'tis’tis a turning from darkneſſedarkness to light.

2. The Subjectsubject changed, and converted, is the whole man; 'tis’tis both the ſinnerssinner'ssinners heart and life: firſtfirst his heart, then his life; firſtfirst his perſonperson, then his practice and converſationconversation. WaſhWash yeeye, make you cleaneclean; there's the change of their perſonspersons; put away the evillevil of your doings from before mine eyes; ceaſecease to doedo evillevil, learnelearn to do well; there's the change of their practiſespracticespractises: So CaſtCast away (ſaithsaith Ezekiel) all your tranſgreſſionstransgressions, whereby you have tranſgreſſedtransgressed; there's the change of the life; and make you a new heart, and a new ſpiritspirit, there's the change of thethe heart.

3. The TearmesTerms of this change, and converſionconversion from which, and to which, both heart and life muſtmust be changed from all ſinsin, to God; the heart muſtmust be changed from the ſtatestate and power of ſinsin, the life from the acts of ſinsin, but both unto God, the heart to be under his power in a ſtatestate of grace, the life to be under his rule, in all new obedience, as the Apoſtleapostle ſpeaksspeaks, To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkneſſedarkness to light, and from the power of ſatansatan unto God: ſoso the Prophetprophet IſaiahIsaiah ſaithsaith, Let the wicked forſakeforsake their wayesways, and the unrighteous man his thoughts, and let him returnereturn unto the Lord. Thus much of the nature of Evangelicallevangelical Repentancerepentance. Now ſoulessouls, tell me whitherwhether it be ſuchsuch an eaſieeasy thing to repent, as Satan doth ſuggeſtsuggest; beſidesbesides what hath been ſpokenspoken, I deſiredesire that you will take notice, that Repentancerepentance doth include a turning from the moſtmost darling ſinsin: Ephraim ſhallshall ſaysay, What have I to doedo any more with Idolsidols? Yea, it's a turning from all ſinsin to God. Ezek. 18. 30. Therefore I will judge you, O HouſeHouse of IſraelIsrael, every one according to his wayesways, ſaithsaith the Lord God: repent, and turneturn your ſelvesselves from all your tranſgreſſionstransgressions: ſoso iniquity ſhallshall not be your ruineruin. Herod turn'd from many, but turn'd not from his Herodias, which was his ruineruin; Judas turn'd
from all viſiblevisible wickedneswickedness, yet he would not caſtcast out that golden Devildevil Covetouſneſſecovetousness, and therefore was caſtcast into the hotteſthottest place in Hellhell. He that turnesturns not from every ſinsin, turnesturns not aright from any one ſinsin; every ſinsin ſtrikesstrikes at the Honourhonour of God, the Being of God, the Gloryglory of God, the Heartheart of ChriſtChrist, the Joyjoy of the Spirit, and the Peacepeace of a mansman's Conſcienceconscience; and therefore a ſoulsoul truly penitent, ſtrikesstrikes at all, hates all, conflicts with all; and will labour to draw ſtrengthstrength from a crucified ChriſtChrist to crucifie • crucify all; a true penitent knowesknows neither father nor mother, neither right eye, nor right hand, but will pluck out the one, and cut off the other. Saul ſparedspared but one Aga • g, and that coſtcost him his ſoulsoul and his Kingdomekingdom: beſidesbesides, Repentancerepentance is not onelyonly a turning from all ſinsin, but alſoalso a turning to all good, to a love of all good, to a prizing of all good, and to a following after all good. Ezek. 18. 21. But if the wicked will turneturn from all his ſinssins that he hath committed, and keep all my Statutesstatutes, and doedo that which is lawfulllawful and right, he ſhallshall ſurelysurely live, behe ſhallshall not die; that is, onelyonly negative righteouſneſſerighteousness and holineſſeholiness is no righteouſneſſerighteousness nor holineſſeholiness; David fulfilled all the wills of God, and had reſpectrespect unto all his Commandementscommandments, and ſoso had
Zacharias and Elizabeth. 'Tis’tis’Tis not enough that the Treetree bears not ill fruit; but, it muſtmust bring forth good fruit, elſeelse, it muſtmust be cut downedown, and eaſtcasteast into the fire: So, 'tis’tis not enough that you are not thus and thus wicked, but you muſtmust be thus and thus gracious, and good, elſeelse Divinedivine Juſticejustice will put the Axeaxe of Divinedivine Vengeancevengeance to the root of your ſoulssouls, and cut you off for ever. Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit, is hewn downedown, and caſtcast into the fire; beſidesbesides, Repentancerepentance doth include a ſenſibleneſſesensibleness of ſinssin'ssins ſinfulneſſesinfulness, how oppoſiteopposite and contrary 'tis’tis to the bleſſedblessed God: God is light, ſinsin is darkneſſedarkness, God is life, ſinsin is death, God is Heavenheaven, ſinsin is hell, God is beauty, ſinsin is deformity. AlſoAlso true Repentancerepentance includes a ſenſiblenessensibleness of ſinssin'ssins miſchievouſneſſemischievousness, how it caſtcast Angelsangels out of Heavenheaven, and Adam out of ParadiſeParadise; how it laid the firſtfirst corner-ſtonestone in hell, and brought in all the curſescurses, croſſescrosses, and miſeriesmiseries, that be in the world, and how it makes men liable to all temporalltemporal, ſpirituallspiritual, and eternalleternal wrath; how it hath made men GodleſſeGodless, ChriſtleſſeChristless, hopeleſſehopeless, and heavenleſſeheavenless in this world: further, true repentance doth include ſorrowsorrow for ſinsin, contrition of heart; it breaks the heart with ſighessighs and ſobssobs, and groans, for that a loving God, and Father is by ſinsin
offended, a bleſſedblessed Saviour a freſhfreshafresh crucified, and the ſweetsweet Comforter, the Spirit,True repentance is a ſorrowingsorrowing for ſinsin as it is offenſivumoffensivum Dei, averſivumaversivum à Deo, this both comes from God, & drives a man to God, as it did the Church in the Canticles, and the ProdigallProdigal. Ezek. 20. 22, 23. grieved and vexed. Again, Repentancerepentance doth include, not onelyonly a loathing of ſinsin, but alſoalso a loathing of our ſelvesselves for ſinsin; as a man doth not onelyonly loathloathe poyſonpoison, but he loathsloathes the very diſhdish or veſſelvessel that hath the ſmellsmell of the poyſonpoison: ſoso a true Penitentpenitent doth not onelyonly loathloathe his ſinsin, but he loathsloathes himſelfehimself, the veſſelvessel that ſtillstill ſmelssmellssmels of ſinsin. So Ezek. 20. 43. And there ſhallshall ye remember your wayesways and all your doings, wherein yeeye have been defiled; and ye ſhallshall loathloathe your ſelvesselves in your owneown ſightsight, for all your evillsevils that ye have committed; true Repentancerepentance will work your hearts, not onelyonly to loathloathe your ſinssins, but alſoalso to loathloathe your ſelvesselves. AgaineAgain, true Repentancerepentance doth not onelyonly work a man to loathloathe himſelfhimself for his ſinssins, but it makes him aſham'dasham'd of his ſinsin alſoalso. What fruit have ye of thoſethose things, whereof ye are (now) aſhamedashamed? ſaithSaith the Apoſtleapostle: ſoso Ezekiel, And thou ſhaltshalt be confounded, and never open thy mouth any more, becauſebecause of thy ſhameshame, when I am pacified toward thee, for all that thou haſthast done, ſaithsaith the Lord God. When a peni • tentiallpenitential ſoulsoul ſeessees his ſinssins pardoned, the anger of God pacified, and Divinedivine Juſticejustice ſatisfiedsatisfied, then he ſitssits down (and bluſhesblushes, as the Hebrew hath it) as one
aſhamedashamed; yea, true Repentancerepentance doth Quantum diſplicetdisplicet Deo immunditia peccati •• , in tantum placet deo eruhiſcentiaerubescentiaeruhiscentia poenitentis. Ber. i. e. So much the more God hath been diſpleaſeddispleased with the blackneſſeblackness of ſinsin, the more will he be pleaſedpleased with the bluſhingblushing of the ſinnersinner. They that do not burn now in zealezeal againſtagainst ſinsin, muſtmust ere long burneburn in Hell for ſinsin. work a man to croſſecross his ſinfullsinful ſelfself, and to walk contrary to ſinfullsinful ſelfeself, to take a holy revenge upon ſinsin, as you may ſeesee in Paul, the JaylorJailer, Mary Magdalen, and ManaſſesManasses; this the Apoſtleapostle ſhewesshows in that 2 Cor. 7. 10, 11. For godly ſorrowsorrow worketh repentance never to be repented of, but the ſorrowsorrow of the world worketh death; for behold the ſelfeſameselfsameselfesame thing that ye ſorrowedsorrowed after a Godly ſortsort, what carefullneſſecarefulnesscarefullness it wrought in you; yea, what clearing of your ſelvesselves; yea, what indignation; yea, what fearefear; yea, what vehement deſiredesire; yea, what zealezeal; yea, what revenge. Now ſoulssouls, ſumsum up all theſethese things together, and tell me, whether it be ſuchsuch an eaſieeasy thing to repent, as Satan would make the ſoulsoul to beleevebelieve; and I am confident your hearts will anſweranswer, that 'tis’tis as hard a thing to repent, as 'tis’tis to make a world, or to raiſeraise the dead. I ſhallshall conclude this ſecondsecond Remedyremedy, with a worthy ſayingsaying of a precious holy man, Repentancerepentance (ſaithsaith he) ſtripsstrips us ſtarkstark naked of all the garments of the old Adam, and leaves not ſoso much as the ſhirtshirt behind; in this rotten building it leaves not a ſtonestone upon a ſtonestone. As the Floodflood drowned Noa'hsNoah's own friends, and ſervantsservants: ſoso muſtmust the flood of repenting tears drown our ſweeteſtsweetest, and moſtmost profitable ſinssins.

The third Remedyremedy againſtagainst this Devicedevice3 Remedy. of Satan, is, ſeriouſlyseriously to conſiderconsider, that Repentancerepentance is a continued act; the word Repentrepent, implies the continuation of it. True Repentancerepentance inclines a mansman's AnſelmeAnselm in his Meditations confeſſethconfesseth, that all his life was either damnable for ſinsin committed, or unprofitable for good omitted and at laſtlast concludes (Quid reſtatrestat o peccato • r niſinisi ut in tota vita tua deplores totam vitam tuam) Oh what then remainesremains, but in our whole life, to lament the ſinssins of our whole life. heart to perform GodsGod's Statutesstatutes always, even unto the end; a true Penitentpenitent muſtmust goego on, from Faithfaith, to Faithfaith, from ſtrengthstrength to ſtrengthstrength, he muſtmust never ſtandstand ſtillstill, nor turneturn back; Repentancerepentance is a grace, and muſtmust have its daily operation, as well as other graces; true Repentancerepentance is a continued ſpringspring, where the waters of godly ſorrowsorrow are alwayesalways flowing; My ſinssins are ever before me; a true penitent is often caſtingcasting his eyes back to the dayesdays of his former vanity, and this makes him morning and evening to water his couch with his tears: Remember not againſtagainst me the ſinssins of my youth, ſaithsaith one bleſſedblessed Penitentpenitent; and I was a blaſphemerblasphemer, and a perſecuterpersecutorpersecuter, and injurious, ſaithsaith another Penitentpenitent: Repentancerepentance is a continued act of turning, a Repentancerepentance never to be repented of, a turning never to turneturn again to folly; a true penitent hath ever ſomethingsomething within him to turn fromfrom; he can never get near enough to God, no, not ſoso near him as once he was; and therefore he is ſtillstill turning and turning, that he may get nearer and nearer to him; that is his chiefeſtchiefest
good, and his onelyonly happineſſehappiness (optimum 'Tis’Tis’tis truly ſaidsaid of God, that he is omnia ſupersuper omnia.
maximum) the beſtbest, and the greateſtgreatest; they are every day a crying out, O wretched men that we are, who ſhallshall deliver us from this body of death? They are ſtillstill ſenſiblesensible of ſinsin, and ſtillstill conflicting with ſinsin, and ſtillstill ſorrowingsorrowing for ſinsin, and ſtillstill loathing of themſelvesthemselves for ſinsin; Repentancerepentance is no tranſienttransient act, but a continued act of the ſoulsoul; and tell me, oh tempted ſoulesoul! whetherWhether it be ſuchsuch an eaſieeasy thing, as Satan would make thee believe, to be every day a turning, more and more from ſinsin, and a turning nearer and nearer to God, thy choiceſtchoicest bleſſedneſſeblessedness. A true Penitentpenitent can as eaſilyeasily content himſelfehimself with one act of faith, or one act of love, as he can content himſelfehimself with one act of Repentancerepentance. A JewiſhJewish RabbieRabbiRabby preſſingpressing the practice of Repentancerepentance upon his Diſciplesdisciples, exhorting them to be ſuresure to Repentrepent the day before they dyeddied; one of them replyedreplied, that the day of any mansman's death was very uncertaineuncertain; Repentrepent therefore, every day (ſaidsaid the Rabbin) and then you ſhallshall be ſuresure to repent the day before you dyedie; you are wiſewise, and know how to apply it to your own advantage.

The fiftfifth Remedyremedy againſtagainst this Devicedevice5 Remedy. of Satan, is, ſeriouſlyseriously to conſiderconsider, that to repent of ſinsin is as great a work of grace, as not to ſinsin. By our ſinfullsinful falls the powers of the ſoulesoul are weaknedweakened, theYet it is better to be kept from ſinsin, thenthan cur • ed of ſinsin by Repentance, as it is better for a man to be preſervedpreserved from a diſeaſedisease thenthan to be cured of the diſeaſedisease. ſtrengthstrength of grace is decayed, our evidences for Heavenheaven are blotted, fearesfears and doubts in the ſoulsoul are raiſedraised (will God once more pardon this ſcarletscarlet ſinsin, and ſhewshow mercy to this wretched ſoulsoul) and
corruptions in the heart are more advantaged, and confirmed, and the conſcienceconscience of a man after falls, is the more inragedenraged, or the more benummedbenumbed; now for a ſoulsoul, notwithſtandingnotwithstanding all this, to repent of his falls, this ſhewesshows, that 'tis’tis as great a work of grace to repent of ſinsin, as 'tis’tis not to ſinsin. Repentance is the vomit of the ſoulsoul, and of all PhyſickPhysic, none ſoso difficult, and hard, as 'tis’tis to vomit; the ſamesame means that tends to preſervepreserve the ſoulsoul from ſinsin, the ſamesame means works the ſoulsoul to riſerise by Repentancerepentance, when 'tis’tis fallen into ſinsin: We know, the mercy and loving kindneſſekindness of God, is one ſpeciallspecial means to keep the ſoulsoul from ſinsin, as David ſpakespake, Thy loving kindneſſekindness is alwayesalways before mine eyes, and I have PſalPsal. 26. 3, 4, 5. walked in thy truth; I have not ſatsat with vain perſonspersons, neither will I go in with diſſemblersdissemblers. I have hated the Congregationcongregation of evillevil doers, and will not ſitsit with the wicked: So by the ſamesame means the ſoulsoul is raiſedraised, by Repentancerepentance out of ſinsin, as you may ſ • eesee in Mary Magdalen, who loved much, andLuke 7. 37, 38, 39, &etcc. HoſHos.Hos 6. 1, 2. wept much, becauſebecause much was forgiven her: ſoso thoſethose in HoſeaHosea, Come, let us returnereturn unto the Lord, for he hath tornetorn, and he will healeheal us; he hath ſmittensmitten, and he will bindebind us up: after two dayesdays he will revive us, in the third day he will raiſeraise us up, and we ſhallshall live in his ſightsight; or before his
face, as the Hebrew hath it, i. eeE. ininIn his לפניו 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉
favour, confidence in GodsGod's mercy, and love, that he would heal them, and bind up their wounds, and revive their dejected ſpiritsspirits, and cauſecause them to live in his favour, was that which did work their hearts to repent, and return unto him; I might further ſhewshow you this truth in many other perticularsparticulars; but this may ſufficesuffice: onelyonly remember this in the gnerallgeneral, that there is much of the power of God, and love of God, and faith in God, and fear of God, and care to pleaſeplease God, and zealezeal for the glory of God, requiſiterequisite to work a man to repent2 Cor. 7. 11. of ſinsin, as there is to keep a man from ſinsin, by which you may eaſilyeasily judge, that to repent of ſinsin, is as great a work, as not to ſinsin; and now tell me, oh ſoulsoul! isIs it an eaſieeasy thing not to ſinsin? weWe know then certainly, 'tis’tis not an eaſieeasy thing to repent of ſinsin.

The ſixtsixth Remedyremedy againſtagainst this Devicedevice6 Remedy. of Satan, is, ſeriouſlyseriously to conſiderconsider, that he that now tempts thee to ſinsin, upon this account, that repentance is eaſieeasy, will ere long, to work thee to deſpairedespair, Beda tells of a certain great man, that was admoniſhedadmonished in his ſicknessickness to repent, who anſwer'danswer'd, that he would not repent yet, for if he ſhouldshould recover, his companions would laugh at him, but growing ſickersicker and ſickersicker, his friends preſſedpressed him again to repent; but • thenbut thenbutthen he told them it was toolatetoo late (Quia jam judicatus ſumsum & condemnatus) for now (ſaidsaid he) I am judged, and condemned.
to ſaysay, we are thine, and we muſtmust follow thee; Now Satan will help to work the ſoulsoul to look up, and ſeesee God angry, and to look inward, and ſeesee Conſcienceconscience accuſingaccusing and condemning; and to look downwards, and ſeesee Hellshell'shells mouth open to receive the impenitent ſoulsoul, and all this to render the work of repentance impoſſibleimpossible to the ſoulsoul; what, ſaithsaith Satan, doeſtdoest thou think that that is eaſieeasy which the whole power of grace cannot conquer, while we are in this world? Is it eaſieeasy, ſaithsaith Satan, to turn from ſomesome outward act of ſinsin, to which thou haſthast been addicted? DoſtDost thou not remember that thou haſthast often complained againſtagainst ſuchsuch and ſuchsuch particular ſinssins, and reſolvedresolved to leave them, and yet to this hour thou haſthast not, thou canſtcanst not? What will it then be to turn from every ſinsin? Yea, to mortifiemortify, and cut off thoſethose ſins • sins, thoſethose darling luſtslusts, that are as joyntsjoints and members, that be as right hands, and right eyes? HaſtHast thou not loved thy ſinssins above thy Saviour? HaſtHast thou not preferred earth before Heavenheaven? HaſtHast thou not all along neglected the means of Gracegrace, and deſpiſeddespised the offers of Gracegrace, and vexed the ſpiritspirit of Gracegrace? There would be no end if I ſhouldshould ſetset before thee the infinitinfinite evils that thou haſthast committed, and the innumerable
good ſervicesservices that thou haſthast omitted,As one Lamachus a Commander ſaidsaid, to one of his ſouldierssoldiers, that was brought before him for a misbehaviour, who pleaded he would doedo ſoso no more, ſaithsaith he (Non li cetlicet in bello bis peccare) no man muſtmust offend twice in war: ſoso God will not ſuffersuffer men often to neglect the day of grace. and the frequent checks of thy owneown Conſcienceconscience, that thou haſthast contemned, and therefore thou mayeſtmayest well conclude, that thou canſtcanst never repent, that thou ſhaltshalt never repent; now ſaithsaith Satan, doedo but a little conſiderconsider thy numberleſſenumberless ſinssins, and the greatneſſegreatness of thy ſinssins, the foulneſſefoulness of thy ſinssins, the hainouſneſſeheinousnesshainousness of thy ſinssins, the circumſtancescircumstances of thy ſinssins, and thou ſhaltshalt eaſilyeasily ſeesee, that thoſethose ſinssins that thou thoughteſtthoughtest to be but motes, are indeed mountainesmountains; and is it not now in vain to repent of them? Surely ſaithsaith Satan, if thou ſhouldeſtshouldest ſeekseek repentance and grace with tears, as EſauEsau, thou ſhaltshalt not find it; thy glaſſeglass is out, thy ſunsun is ſetset, the door of mercy is ſhutshut, the golden Scepterscepter is taken in, and now thou that haſthast deſpiſeddespised mercy, ſhaltshalt be for ever deſtroyeddestroyed by Juſticejustice; for ſuchsuch a wretch as thou art to attempt repentance, is to attempt a thing impoſſibleimpossible; 'tis’tis impoſſibleimpossible that thou, that in all thy life couldeſtcouldest never conquer one ſinnesin, ſhouldeſtshouldest maſtermaster ſuchsuch a numberlesnumberless number of ſinssins, which are ſoso near, ſoso dear, ſoso neceſſarynecessary, and ſoso profitable to thee, that have ſoso long bedded and boarded with thee, that have been old acquaintance and companions with thee; haſthast thou not often purpoſedpurposed, promiſedpromised,
vowed, and reſolvedresolved to enter upon theRepentanceisRepentance is a work that muſtmust be timely done, or men are utterly undone for ever. Aut poenitendum aut pereundum. practice of repentance, but to this day couldeſtcouldest never attain it: Surely 'tis’tis in vain to ſtrivestrive againſtagainst the ſtreamestream, where it is ſoso impoſſibleimpossible to overcome; thou art loſtlost, and caſtcast for ever to hell, thou muſtmust to hell, thou ſhaltshalt; ah ſoulssouls! heHe that now tempts you to ſinsin, by ſuggeſtingsuggesting to you the eaſineſſeeasiness of repentance, will at laſtlast, to work you to deſpairedespair, preſentpresent repentance as the hardeſthardest work in all the world, and a work as far above man, as Heavenheaven is above Hellhell, as light is above darkneſſedarkness. Oh! that you were wiſewise, to break off your ſinssins, by timely repentance.

Now the ſeventhseventh Devicedevice that Satan7 Device. hath to draw the ſoulsoul to ſinsin, is, by making the ſoulsoul bold to venture upon the occaſionsoccasions of ſinsin. Saith Satan, you may walk by the Harlotsharlot'sharlots door, though you won't goego into the Harlotsharlot'sharlots bed; you may ſitsit and ſipsip with the drunkard, thothough you won't be drunk with the drunkard; you may look upon JezabelsJezebel's beauty, and you may play and toy with DalilohDelilah, though you doedo not commit wickedneſſewickedness with the one, or the other; you may with Achan handle the golden wedge, though you doedo not ſtealesteal the golden wedge, &etcc.

div.head: Now the Remedies againſtagainst this Device are theſethese that follow.
div.p:
THeThe firſtfirst Remedyremedy, is, ſolemnlysolemnly to1 Remedy. dwell upon thoſethose Scriptures that doedo expreſslyexpressly command us to avoid the occaſionsoccasions of ſinsin, and the leaſtleast appearance of evillevil. 1 TheſſThess. 5. 22. AbſtaineAbstain from all

TheodoſiusTheodosius tare the ArriansArians'Arians Argumentsarguments, preſentedpresented to him in writing, becauſebecause he found them repugnant to the Scriptures; and AuguſtineAugustine retracted even Ironies onelyonly, becauſebecause they had the appearance of lying. When God had commanded the JewesJews to abſtainabstain from SwinesSwine's fleſhflesh, they would not ſoso much as name it, but in their common talk would call a Sow another thing. To abſtainabstain from all appearance of evillevil, is to doedo nothing wherein ſinsin appears, or which hath a ſhadowshadow of ſinsin. Whatever is of an ill ſhewshow, or of ill report, that he may neither wound conſcienceconscience, nor credit; we muſtmust ſhunshun, and be ſhieshy of the very ſhewshow and ſhadowshadow of ſinnesin, if either we tender our credit abroad, or our comfort at home. It was
good counſellcounsel that Livia gave her Husband Socrates ſpeakethspeaketh of two young men that flung away their belts, when being in an IdolsIdol's Temple, the luſtratinglustrating water fell upon them, deteſtingdetesting ſaithsaith the HiſtorianHistorian, the garment ſportedspottedsported by the fleſhflesh. AuguſtusAugustus; it behoveth thee, not onelyonly not to doedo wrong, but not to ſeeemeseemseeeme to doedo ſoso, &etcc. So Jude 23. v. And others ſavesave with fear pulling them out of the fire, hating even the garment ſpottedspotted by the fleſhflesh. 'Tis’Tis a phraſephrase taken from legalllegal uncleaneſſeuncleannessuncleaness, which was contracted by touching the houſeshouses, the veſſellsvessels, the garments of uncleaneunclean perſonspersons.
